title: Not seen for a week
stem:
You are an F2 doctor. Your friend Dr Kemp, another F2, hasn't been at work for a week. She isn't on leave, and she hasn't replied to your messages or calls.

A fortnight ago she told you she was struggling after her relationship ended. She lives alone.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Tell her educational supervisor that you're worried.
options.brief: They need to know, and can contact her or her next of kin.
options.detailed: Her supervisor or the programme office will want to know, and may have contact details for her next of kin.

options.text: Wait a few more days, as she may just need space.
options.brief: Her absence and silence are out of character and concerning.
options.detailed: She may need space, but a week's absence without explanation, after telling you she was struggling, is a cause for concern.

options.text: Post in the foundation doctors' group chat asking if anyone has seen her.
options.detailed: Others may have heard from her, but posting publicly spreads her private situation.

options.text: Go to her flat and ask the landlord to let you in.
options.brief: Not your role, and may not be safe or lawful.
options.detailed: This may seem caring, but entering her home isn't your role. A welfare check by the police is safer.

options.text: Report her absence as unprofessional to the rota coordinator.
options.brief: Treats a welfare concern as a disciplinary issue.
options.detailed: The rota coordinator may need to know, but framing it as unprofessional overlooks your concern for her.

options.text: Try to reach her through a mutual friend or a family member.
options.brief: Someone else may have heard from her.
options.detailed: A friend or family member may know where she is, or be able to check on her.

options.text: Keep messaging her until she replies.
options.detailed: Messaging shows care, but if she isn't replying, others need to know.

options.text: Consider asking the police to check on her welfare.
options.brief: Her silence, recent distress and living alone are concerning.
options.detailed: If you can't reach her and are worried for her safety, the police can carry out a welfare check. Her recent distress and absence make this reasonable.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you act on a concern for a colleague's welfare, escalating appropriately.
explanation.keyDetails: She has been absent for a week, isn't answering, recently disclosed distress, and lives alone.
explanation.reasoning: [A] informs those responsible, [F] uses her network, and [H] considers a welfare check. The distractors delay ([B], [G]), spread her situation ([C]), overstep ([D]), or misframe it ([E]).
explanation.competing: [B] is the tempting option because she may want space, but her circumstances make it too risky to wait.
